segments: This article primarily uses Bash-style syntax. Fish differs in its syntax for variables, command substitution, history, and configuration.

The previous three articles covered "which commands to use"; this one covers "how to join them together". Pipes and redirection put the Linux philosophy into practice: small tools combine to do powerful things.
| — Feed one command’s output into the next command
The basic idea: standard output from command1 becomes standard input to command2 directly.
2>&1 — Merge standard error into standard output
2>&1 means: redirect stderr (2) to wherever stdout (1) is currently going.
alias — Give a long command a short name
To make it persistent, put it in ~/.bashrc (bash) or ~/.config/fish/config.fish (fish).
Send EOF (exit the terminal or close the input stream)
Move the cursor to the beginning of the line
Move the cursor to the end of the line
Delete the word before the cursor
Ctrl+R is particularly useful: search a long history for a command you have used, then press it again to continue searching backward.
Solve practical problems with a one-line command
This is the Unix philosophy: have each command do one thing well, and connect them with pipes.
Once you understand this, the ways of connecting commands fall naturally into place.

Redirections are processed from left to right: > output.log 2>&1 and 2>&1 > output.log are not equivalent. History expansions such as !! are available in interactive Bash; check the expanded command before executing it.
